newsitem.title: UK: Gold easier, base metals firmer as markets wind down.
newsitem.headline: Gold easier, base metals firmer as markets wind down.

text.p: Gold was easier on the back of insufficient market momentum on Thursday as business activities slowed down ahead of Christmas holidays, and cocoa's recovery from a one-month low experienced lack of follow-through.
"Activity is slowing down and business has been very quiet. We have not seen any real new trend in gold so far," said an analyst based in continental Europe.
Gold closed at $368.80/369.30 per ounce compared with Wednesday's close of $368.85/$369.35.
Dealers said there was no clear trend in the price overnight as the market steadily slowed down ahead of the holidays next week.
"No new business is expected before Christmas. The producers and funds have done what they had to do and industrial interest will not be back before January," one market professional said.
London cocoa futures eased back as the market resumed its range after failing to to follow through to Wednesday's rally.
"The market has failed to show any ability to move up," said one trader.
London cocoa March futures finished at 905 stg against Wednesday's close of 912 stg.
Base metals ticked higher on the back of firmer copper prices, which ended the day with three months delivery at $2,155 against Wednesday's close of $2,114.
"There's been some speculative buying and possibly light fund buying as the spreads tighten," said a trader, adding that the buying was a combination of shortcovering and fresh buying.
In other news, Britain's top financial watchdog, Securities and Investments Board (SIB) told the London Metal Exchange (LME) to provide more information and tighten regulation.
The SIB was asked by the world's biggest market for industrial metals to carry out a top-to-bottom review of the LME after the Sumitomo scandal shocked metal markets in June.
In mid-June, Sumitomo Corp of Japan fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he had admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.
In coffee, traders mostly discounted fears that Mexican coffee areas might be threatened by frost, saying that small crop losses of between one and five percent could be expected.
"That (the Mexican news) is keeping the market supported, but nobody is placing too much importance on it," said one trader.
"The damage, if happens, will only be in limited areas," said the trader.
Snow fell on the mountains outside Mexico City on Thursday while coffee growing belts saw temperatures above freezing and recorded light rains, meterologists said.
